Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

vignette: As she stood on the worn deck of her ship, Captain Sophia Jensen gazed out at the sea with a mixture of nostalgia and unease. The salty air carried memories of her late husband, who had been by her side for decades as they navigated the world's oceans together. But it also reminded her of that fateful day when their lives took a drastic turn - the day she was brutally handled by police during a protest against maritime pollution. Sophia's mind would often wander back to the events of that day, reliving the fear and helplessness as if it were happening all over again. Her memories of the incident were vivid, like photographs etched into her brain - the sound of batons cracking on shields, the feeling of being pinned against a wall, and the sight of her husband's anguished face as he tried to intervene. The more she dwelled on these images, the more they seemed to sear themselves into her mind. To keep these memories at bay, Sophia found herself throwing herself into work with an intensity that bordered on obsession. She would spend hours poring over navigational charts and monitoring weather reports, trying to exhaust herself so that when she finally retired to her quarters, she wouldn't be haunted by the ghosts of the past. But even as she worked tirelessly, her mind would inevitably wander back to the event - rehashing why it had happened to her, replaying every moment in a futile attempt to make sense of the chaos. This relentless rumination became a self-perpetuating cycle: the more Sophia dwelled on the traumatic memories, the more she felt compelled to work herself into exhaustion; and the more exhausted she was, the harder it seemed to shake off the vivid recollections that tormented her. As time went by, Sophia began to notice the toll this cycle took on her daily life - the way her usually keen mind grew foggy with fatigue, and how her once-sturdy body ached from lack of rest. Despite these physical consequences, Sophia struggled to break free from the loop. She would often catch herself going over and over the events leading up to the police violence, trying to pinpoint what she might have done differently - a futile exercise that left her feeling trapped in an endless labyrinth of "what ifs" and "maybes". As the months passed, Sophia's ship began to show signs of neglect, its once-pristine decks now weathered from disuse. Her crew grew concerned about her increasing absence from command duties, sensing the weight of unspoken struggles that had begun to erode their captain's normally formidable spirit. Sophia knew she couldn't keep running from her memories forever - but every time she tried to confront them head-on, they seemed to come flooding back with renewed force. Now, at 76, she felt like a ship adrift in treacherous waters, unsure how much longer she could hold on before being pulled under by the undertow of her own trauma. As she stood on the deck, the wind whipping her silver hair into a frenzy, Sophia knew that she needed help to break this cycle - or risk losing herself completely to the memories that haunted her.
